revisions.title: Courtesy and examination
revisions.body: Socrates opens with honorific praise, but the conversation quickly asks what wisdom can do in public and private life. Hippias answers by assigning the ancients an incapacity; Socrates then proposes, for examination, that sophistic art has progressed beyond them. I read the opening’s courtesy as compatible with a test, not proof that a concealed test is already the scene’s settled design.

revisions.title: Sparta as the pressure point
revisions.body: Socrates turns an earnings-based measure of wisdom into a test of Hippias’s claim that his wisdom improves learners in virtue. Sparta is the pressure point: Hippias says he earned nothing there, and Socrates asks how that fits his expertise claim. The questioning proceeds by forced alternatives, then extends the test through a horsemanship analogy. Hippias offers ancestral custom as an explanation; the passage does not yet settle the tension.

revisions.title: Law, benefit, and a conditional reversal
revisions.body: The conversation turns from Hippias’s earnings to law’s relation to benefit. After Hippias accepts that the more beneficial is, in truth, more lawful, Socrates applies the premise to Sparta: if Hippias’s foreign education benefits Spartan sons more, then his own account makes it more lawful than their fathers’ teaching. Read as an argument, this is conditional—not a settled verdict that Sparta is unlawful or that Hippias’s teaching is actually superior.

revisions.title: Practice before conclusion
revisions.body: Here Hippias’s claim of an easy lesson is converted into a practice procedure. Socrates asks permission to imitate the earlier questioner by objecting to Hippias’s answers, and Hippias consents. That arrangement makes the ensuing beautiful-by-beauty formulation something to test: it is posed in the exchange, not yet established as either speaker’s conclusion.
